passage:
Sahil, you look like the world has ended. Let me tell you what happened to me. I'm Farida, and at twenty-one, two days before my final project was due, my laptop died and the only copy went with it. I sat on the hostel stairs shaking. My roommate Uzma sat beside me and asked, "How much will this matter in a year?"
I said, "Everything." She said, "To whom?" I thought: my professor, my parents, me. In a year my professor would have marked forty other projects. My parents would care that I was well. I would care that I had finished something.
It still hurt. But the crash felt smaller, and I went to my professor that evening and asked for two extra days. She gave me one. I rewrote it in twenty hours and passed.

qa.q: How many extra days did Farida ask for, and how many did she get?
qa.a: Farida asked for two extra days and the professor gave one.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling on the hostel stairs?
qa.a: Farida was panicked and in deep distress, shaking and saying the crash mattered to everything. The fear was real, not just drama.

qa.q: What turning point in the story let Farida act instead of freezing?
qa.a: Uzma's questions about how much it would matter in a year, and to whom. Working through them made the problem smaller and let Farida go and ask the professor for time.

qa.q: Why might Uzma have asked questions and not simply said everything would be fine?
qa.a: Uzma could see that Farida's pain was real. The questions let Farida do the zooming out without being told how, which plain reassurance could not have done. 🤍

grounding: An elder recalls asking how much a disaster would matter in a year and to whom, which cut the drama without denying the pain.

Rain had ripped the tarp off the fest stall at 7:40 am, and the gates opened at 9. Shankar stood in a puddle, holding a sodden banner, his jaw tight. Every poster he had painted for two weeks was smeared. "It's ruined," he said. "Everything's ruined."
Kavitha, stapling a spare cloth to the frame beside him, didn't tell him to calm down. "Okay. In a year, who will remember this?" Shankar laughed shakily. "Me. Probably my parents, because I'll tell them." "And who would have noticed the posters?" "Maybe the first ten people who walk by."
He wiped his face. It still stung. But he picked up the marker and started on a fresh sign with a bigger, simpler design, and by 8:55 it was drying under the cloth.

qa.q: What time did the gates open?
qa.a: The gates opened at 9.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling as he stood in the puddle holding the ruined banner?
qa.a: He was hurt and overwhelmed. His tight jaw and his declaring everything ruined show how much the two weeks of work meant to him.

qa.q: What small step got Shankar moving again?
qa.a: Answering Kavitha's questions about who would remember shrank the disaster, so he picked up a marker and started a simpler sign.

qa.q: How might Kavitha have felt while Shankar was upset and time was running out?
qa.a: Kavitha was probably worried and focused. Kavitha kept stapling the cloth rather than telling Shankar to calm down, which respects his feelings while helping with the deadline.

grounding: A young adult facing a fest-stall disaster asks how much it will matter in a year and to whom; the pain remains but shrinks.

passage: By eleven the rain had flattened the stall. Rukmini stood in the college quadrangle holding a soggy cardboard sign, VEGAN BAKES, while sixty cupcakes she had baked through the night dissolved into the mud. Mahima dragged the plastic sheet off the table. "Ruks, come inside." "Everyone saw," Rukmini said. "The whole fest. I told the committee it would be the best stall." In the canteen she drank hot chai with shaking hands. Then she did something Mahima had seen her do before exams: she stared at the wall and asked, out loud, "Okay. In one year, who will remember this? And who does it actually hurt?" She counted on her fingers. "Me. The committee, a little. Nobody else." She still looked miserable. "It's awful today," she said. "But it's today."

qa.q: How many cupcakes had Rukmini baked through the night?
qa.a: She had baked sixty cupcakes.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling as she drank chai in the canteen?
qa.a: She was upset and embarrassed, worried that the whole fest had seen her stall fail after she had promised it would be the best.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking who would remember it in a year and who it actually hurt worked, because it shrank the disaster to its real size without pretending it didn't sting.

qa.q: How might Mahima see Rukmini's way of coping?
qa.a: Mahima has seen her do this before exams, so she probably feels reassured that Rukmini is using a habit that helps her.

grounding: Shows a young adult zooming out in time and space after a public disaster, easing the drama while still admitting the pain.

"Didi, I didn't get it. The final round. They took two people and I wasn't one."
"Oh, Pankaj. I'm sorry. Where are you?"
"Outside the campus. Sitting on the scooter. I can't go back to the hostel, everyone's celebrating."
"Stay on the phone with me. How bad does it feel?"
"Like the whole of fourth year was a waste."
Manjula didi was quiet, then said, "Can I ask something annoying?"
"You always do."
"A year from now, where do you think this matters?"
"...In my head, mostly. Amma and Appa will be disappointed tonight. By next year? There'll be other interviews."
"And the two who got picked?"
"They'll be busy with their jobs. Nobody will remember I was in the room."
"So it's a bad night."
"A really bad night," Pankaj said. His voice was steadier. "Okay. I'll go back."

qa.q: How many people were taken in the final round?
qa.a: They took two people.

qa.q: How can you tell Pankaj felt a little steadier by the end of the call?
qa.a: His voice became steadier, and he moved from calling fourth year a waste to calling it 'a really bad night' and agreeing to go back to the hostel.

qa.q: Which part of Manjula's approach helped most, and why?
qa.a: She stayed on the phone, asked how bad it felt first, and only then asked the 'one year from now' question, so he did the zooming out himself.

qa.q: How might Pankaj's parents be affected by the news?
qa.a: Pankaj expects Amma and Appa to feel disappointed tonight, though by next year it will probably be a small part of a longer job search.

grounding: Shows a young adult asking how much a setback will matter in a year and to whom, easing the drama while admitting it hurts.

passage:
Two hundred people, a microphone, and my mind went completely white.
I was presenting our club's water-filter idea at the college innovation summit. I got as far as "Good morning, esteemed judges" and then nothing. Twenty seconds of nothing. Someone coughed. I read the rest off my phone like a robot.
Afterwards I sat on the steps behind the auditorium and wanted to disappear. Wasim sat down next to me with two samosas.
"Raghav," he said, "in a year, who's going to talk about this?"
I thought about it properly. The judges had seen forty teams. My club mates were already arguing about lunch. My parents would hear the funny version.
"Honestly? Me," I said.
It still burned. It still burns a bit now. But on those steps, it became one bad morning instead of my whole reputation.

qa.q: How long did Raghav's mind stay blank?
qa.a: Twenty seconds of nothing.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel sitting on the steps behind the auditorium?
qa.a: Raghav felt humiliated and wanted to disappear after blanking in front of two hundred people.

qa.q: What small step could Raghav take before the next presentation?
qa.a: Raghav could practise the opening lines aloud in front of a couple of friends so the first minute feels automatic under pressure.

qa.q: How does Wasim seem to see the disaster?
qa.a: Wasim seems to see it as a painful but passing moment, bringing samosas and asking the one-year question instead of dismissing Raghav's feelings.

grounding: Shows a young adult zooming out in time and to other people after freezing on stage, which cuts the drama without denying the sting.

passage:
Hostel warden's log, Block C, Wednesday, 11 pm.
Chetan came to the office pale, laptop in hand. His final-year project drive had failed two days before submission. He kept saying, "It's over, everything's over." His roommate Shankar came with him. I made tea and let him talk. After a while I asked what I ask everyone in that chair: "A year from now, who will remember this, and how much?" He went quiet, then counted on his fingers: his guide, himself, maybe his parents. "The guide will remember whether I told him early," he said. That seemed to steady him. He agreed to email the guide that night and ask about an extension. Shankar offered his old laptop and the printed drafts. I checked in at 8 am. The email had gone, and the guide had replied.

qa.q: How many days before submission did Chetan's drive fail?
qa.a: It failed two days before submission.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he arrived at the office?
qa.a: He felt panicked and hopeless, pale and repeating that everything was over.

qa.q: Which question helped Chetan, and why?
qa.a: Asking who would remember this in a year, and how much, shrank the disaster to a few people and pointed him to one step: telling his guide early.

qa.q: How might Shankar have felt standing beside Chetan that night?
qa.a: Shankar was probably worried for his roommate and glad to be useful, offering his old laptop and the printed drafts.

grounding: Shows a young adult facing a project disaster zooming out to a year ahead, which calms the panic without pretending the loss is small.
